name: Pohara
headline: Holiday homes in Pōhara
metaDescription: Book a Pohara holiday home a short walk from the beach — family baches, studios and big houses, 10 minutes from Takaka. Pet-friendly options and local support.
intro: Pōhara is Golden Bay's main beach settlement: ten minutes east of Tākaka on Abel Tasman Drive, with a long north-facing beach, a campground at one end and Tarakohe Harbour around the point at the other. It has more holiday homes than anywhere else in the Bay, most of them a two- or three-minute walk from the sand. It is also the only place here where you can park the car on Friday and not touch it again until you leave.
body:
Pōhara suits families and multi-generational groups better than anywhere else in Golden Bay — the biggest houses are here, the walk to the water is flat, and Tākaka's supermarket, bakery and cafés are a ten-minute drive rather than a half-hour expedition. Guests arrive with kids, bikes, boogie boards and often a dog, and the reviews say much the same three things every summer: they walked to the beach before breakfast, the tidal flats kept the little ones busy for hours, and they barely used the car.

It is also the closest holiday-home base to the northern end of the Abel Tasman. The Wainui Bay car park at the top of the Coast Track is about fifteen minutes further along the coast, the boat ramp at Tarakohe is just around the headland, and the Grove Scenic Reserve is a short detour on the way back into town. Plenty of the Pōhara homes take dogs, so filter for pets if yours is coming — and if you want a sea view rather than a beach walk, look at the houses set up on the hill behind the road.
highlights: Closest beach settlement to Tākaka — about 10 minutes to the supermarket, fuel and cafés
Long, gently shelving beach; at low tide the sand flats run out far enough for children to wade for an hour
Tarakohe Harbour and its boat ramp are around the headland, the launching point for fishing and dive trips
About 15 minutes to the Wainui Bay track head at the northern end of the Abel Tasman
The widest choice of homes in the Bay, from two-person studios to houses that sleep eleven or more

faqs.q: How far is Pōhara from Takaka?
faqs.a: About 10 km, or a 10-minute drive along Abel Tasman Drive. Tākaka has the only supermarket in Golden Bay, plus the pharmacy, petrol and most of the cafés, so it is worth doing one big shop on the way in.

faqs.q: Can you swim at Pōhara at low tide?
faqs.a: Yes, you just walk out further. Golden Bay has a large tidal range, so at low water the flats extend a long way and the shallows sit bath-warm through January and February. If you want deep water off the beach — or you are launching a boat — check a Tarakohe or Nelson tide chart and aim for the couple of hours either side of high tide.

faqs.q: Are dogs allowed on Pōhara Beach?
faqs.a: Many of our Pōhara homes are pet-friendly and the beach is a popular dog walk, but Tasman District Council applies seasonal and time-of-day rules to parts of it. Read the signs at the beach accesses, keep the dog on a lead near the campground end, and pick up after them on the reserve.

faqs.q: What is the drive in like?
faqs.a: Everyone comes over Takaka Hill on SH60 — roughly two hours from Nelson and a little over an hour from Motueka, on a sealed but tightly winding road that slows to a crawl behind campervans in summer. Allow more time than the map suggests, fill up before you cross, and expect the phone signal to drop out on the way.

name: Collingwood
headline: Holiday homes in Collingwood
metaDescription: Collingwood holiday homes at the far end of Golden Bay — the base for Farewell Spit tours and Wharariki Beach, 25 minutes from Takaka. Waterfront and village stays.
intro: Collingwood sits where the Aorere River empties into Ruataniwha Inlet, twenty-five minutes past Tākaka and the last real village before Farewell Spit. It is small — a tavern, a café or two, a general store and a fuel pump — and that is precisely the appeal. The tide runs hard through the inlet in front of town, so mornings here are about wading birds, driftwood and the light coming off the Kahurangi ranges rather than surf.
body:
People who choose Collingwood are usually here for the far end of the Bay. Farewell Spit tours leave from the village, Wharariki Beach and the Cape Farewell seal colony are about forty-five minutes on, and the tracks through Milnthorpe Park are ten minutes back down the coast road. Walkers, birdwatchers, fishers and anyone who wants their phone to stop working for a week tend to book here — the reviews are almost always about quiet: hearing the tide turn, the stars, the kids fishing off the wharf.

The trade-off is distance. Pōhara and Tata Beach are about forty minutes away, so it pays to plan days around one end of Golden Bay at a time rather than criss-crossing it. Collingwood has a store and fuel, but the full supermarket shop is still in Tākaka, and a couple of our Collingwood houses look straight across the water — worth checking the outlook before you pick one, because the estuary view changes completely between tides.
highlights: Departure point for Farewell Spit tours — the only legal way to travel the length of the Spit
About 45 minutes to Wharariki Beach, the seal pups and the Archway Islands
Ruataniwha Inlet on the doorstep: kayaking and wading birds on a rising tide, sandflats on a falling one
Milnthorpe Park's walking and biking tracks are ten minutes back toward Tākaka
A general store, fuel, a tavern and a café — the last services before Cape Farewell

faqs.q: How far is Collingwood from Takaka?
faqs.a: About 26 km, or a 25-minute drive on SH60 along the coast through Onekakā and Parapara. Tākaka still has the nearest supermarket, pharmacy and the widest choice of cafés.

faqs.q: Is Collingwood good for swimming?
faqs.a: Not in the way Pōhara or Tata Beach are. The village sits on a tidal inlet that drains to sandflats, so swimming is a high-tide activity here. For a proper beach day, Patons Rock and Parapara are fifteen and ten minutes back down the coast. Wharariki, up the far end, is spectacular but exposed and not a swimming beach.

faqs.q: Do I need to book a Farewell Spit tour in advance?
faqs.a: Yes, especially between December and February. Departures are tide-dependent, so the time moves day to day and seats are limited — book before you arrive and build the rest of that day around the departure time.

faqs.q: Is there mobile coverage out this way?
faqs.a: Patchy, and it depends on your network. Treat Wharariki Beach, Farewell Spit and the back roads toward the Aorere Valley as no-signal country: download offline maps before you leave the village. Our Collingwood homes have wifi, so you can still check in with the world from the deck.

name: Tata Beach
headline: Holiday homes at Tata Beach
metaDescription: Tata Beach holiday homes on Golden Bay's safest swimming bay — sheltered sand, kayaks off the beach, no through traffic, 20 minutes from Takaka.
intro: Tata Beach is a crescent of pale sand looking out at the two Tata Islands, twenty minutes east of Tākaka past Pōhara and Ligar Bay. There is no shop, no café and no through traffic — the road stops in the settlement — which is exactly why the same families come back to the same house every January. The bay is shallow and sheltered by the islands, so it is a paddling, kayaking and swimming beach rather than a surf one.
body:
This is the quietest of Golden Bay's popular beaches and the homes reflect it: fewer of them, generally larger, and several set up in the bush on the Tata headlands with long decks and views straight down the bay. Guests searching for safe swimming, kayaks and no road noise end up here, and reviews mention the same things — the water was flat every morning, the kids could be sent to the beach on their own, nobody heard a car all week.

Golden Bay Kayaks operates from the beach itself, so guided trips and rentals start a few metres from the sand, and the Abel Tasman coastline begins around the corner. Because there is nothing to buy in the settlement, do a full shop in Tākaka on the way through and bring the chilly bin; most guests only leave for the Wainui Falls walk ten minutes away, or to drive back to Pōhara for dinner.
highlights: Sheltered, shallow bay — one of the safest swimming beaches in Golden Bay for small children
Golden Bay Kayaks runs guided trips and rentals from the beach itself
No shops in the settlement; Tākaka, 20 minutes away, has the nearest supermarket
Wainui Falls, the Bay's most popular short waterfall walk, is a 10-minute drive
The road ends here — almost no passing traffic, and genuinely dark skies at night

faqs.q: Is Tata Beach good for young children?
faqs.a: It is the beach most Golden Bay parents name first. The sand shelves gently, the islands take the swell out of anything from the north, and the shallows warm up quickly on an incoming tide. There are no lifeguards anywhere in Golden Bay, so the usual rules apply — and at low tide you will walk out a long way before it is deep enough to swim.

faqs.q: Where is the nearest shop or café?
faqs.a: Pōhara is about eight minutes back around the coast for a meal or a coffee, and Tākaka is twenty minutes away for the supermarket, bakery and fuel. There is nothing commercial at Tata Beach itself, so stock up before you arrive.

faqs.q: Can I launch a kayak or boat at Tata Beach?
faqs.a: Kayaks, paddleboards and small craft go straight off the sand, which is one of the reasons the settlement is so popular with paddlers. For a trailer boat, use the sealed ramp at Tarakohe Harbour near Pōhara, about fifteen minutes away.

faqs.q: How do I get into the Abel Tasman from Tata Beach?
faqs.a: The northern trailhead at Wainui Bay is about fifteen minutes by road, and the Wainui Falls track is on the way. Water taxis and most track transport run from Mārahau at the southern end, which is an hour and a half back over Takaka Hill — so many guests take a kayak day trip from Tata instead.

name: Patons Rock
headline: Holiday homes at Patons Rock
metaDescription: Patons Rock holiday homes on a long, quiet Golden Bay beach — sunsets over the water, horse treks up the road, midway between Takaka and Collingwood.
intro: Patons Rock is a long, quiet beach fifteen minutes north of Tākaka, named for the rock outcrop at its southern end. A few dozen houses sit back behind the dunes with a grass reserve and beach access between them, and at low tide the firm sand runs for a couple of kilometres in either direction. Because this stretch of coast faces roughly northwest, the sun sets over the water for most of the summer.
body:
Families with dogs, walkers and kite-flyers do well here. The beach is wide enough that even at New Year you can walk away from everybody, and the shallow water warms fast on an incoming tide. Hack Farm runs horse treks from just up the road and along the sand, which is the single most-mentioned thing in the notes guests leave after staying at Patons Rock.

There is nothing commercial in the settlement, so it is a shop-in-Tākaka kind of stay: fifteen minutes each way for the supermarket, cafés and fuel. Collingwood and the Farewell Spit end of the Bay are fifteen minutes the other way, which makes Patons Rock a genuinely central base — you can do the Spit one day and Pupū Springs or Pōhara the next without either trip feeling long.
highlights: Two-plus kilometres of firm sand at low tide — the pick of the long beach walks in Golden Bay
Beach horse treks with Hack Farm leave from just up the road
Faces northwest, so the sun sets over the water through the summer months
Midway between Tākaka (15 min) and Collingwood (15 min)
No shops, no through traffic and no streetlights

faqs.q: Can I take a dog to Patons Rock Beach?
faqs.a: It is one of the more relaxed dog-walking beaches in Golden Bay, and one of our Patons Rock homes is pet-friendly. Tasman District Council bylaws still apply, including lead-only areas around the reserve and seasonal restrictions, so check the signs at the beach access when you arrive.

faqs.q: Is the swimming safe at Patons Rock?
faqs.a: It is an open, gently shelving beach with no lifeguard patrol anywhere on this coast. The water is calm in most conditions but a northerly puts up a real chop, and the tide moves a long way — swim in the hours either side of high tide and keep an eye on children in the shallows.

faqs.q: How far is Patons Rock from the Abel Tasman and Farewell Spit?
faqs.a: Roughly forty minutes to the Wainui Bay track head at the northern end of the Abel Tasman, and about half an hour to Collingwood for a Farewell Spit tour departure. Being in the middle of the Bay is the point of staying here.

faqs.q: Where is the nearest café or shop?
faqs.a: Tākaka, fifteen minutes south, has the supermarket and the biggest choice of cafés. Collingwood, fifteen minutes north, has a store, fuel, a café and the tavern. There is nothing at Patons Rock itself except the beach.

name: Ligar Bay
headline: Holiday homes at Ligar Bay
metaDescription: Ligar Bay holiday homes between Pohara and Tata Beach — calm swimming across the road, the Abel Tasman Memorial above the bay, five minutes to Pohara.
intro: Ligar Bay is the small bay between Pōhara and Tata Beach: one row of houses on the inland side of Abel Tasman Drive, sand and calm water on the other. The Abel Tasman Memorial stands on the headland above it, marking the 1642 anchorage that gave Golden Bay its first European name. It is a two-minute walk up from the roadside and the best view on this stretch of coast.
body:
Ligar Bay suits people who want Pōhara's convenience without Pōhara's summer buzz. You are five minutes from the shops, café and boat ramp at Pōhara and Tarakohe, five minutes the other way from Tata Beach, and the swimming out front is shallow and sheltered. The two homes we look after here could not be more different — a plain, easy-going cottage a short stroll from the sand, and a landmark tower with a spa and views straight down the bay — so bookings here skew toward couples and small groups rather than big family reunions.

Everything is informal: pull off the road, cross the grass verge, and you are on the beach. There is no shop in the bay, so meals come from Pōhara or from the supermarket in Tākaka, fifteen minutes away. What guests write about afterwards is how still the water is first thing in the morning, and how quickly they got into the habit of walking up to the memorial before dinner.
highlights: Between Pōhara (5 min) and Tata Beach (5 min) — three beaches within a short drive
The Abel Tasman Memorial lookout sits on the headland above the bay
Calm, shallow water directly across the road from the houses
About 10 minutes to Wainui Falls and the northern Abel Tasman track head
Only a couple of dozen baches, so it stays quiet even over New Year

faqs.q: Can you walk from Ligar Bay to Tata Beach?
faqs.a: Not comfortably. It is roughly 2 km on Abel Tasman Drive, which is narrow, winding and has no footpath for much of the way, and a headland separates the two beaches. Almost everyone drives the five minutes.

faqs.q: Where do we eat if we stay at Ligar Bay?
faqs.a: Pōhara, five minutes away, is the nearest food — including the restaurant at Ratanui Lodge. Tākaka's cafés, restaurants and supermarket are about fifteen minutes over the hill, and there is nothing to buy in Ligar Bay itself.

faqs.q: What is the Abel Tasman Memorial?
faqs.a: A memorial on the headland between Ligar Bay and Tarakohe, put up to mark Abel Tasman's ships anchoring off this coast in December 1642. The encounter that followed with local Ngāti Tūmatakōkiri left four of his crew dead, and he named the place Murderers' Bay before sailing on without ever landing. It is a short, steep walk up from the roadside car park.

faqs.q: Is Ligar Bay good for swimming?
faqs.a: Yes — it is one of the calmest bits of water in Golden Bay, shallow and sheltered, which makes it easy with young children. As everywhere here, the tide pulls back a long way, so time a proper swim for the hours around high tide.

name: Parapara
headline: Holiday homes at Parapara
metaDescription: Parapara holiday homes on the quiet coast road between Takaka and Collingwood — beach and estuary swimming, wading birds, dark skies and big Golden Bay views.
intro: Parapara is a scatter of houses on the coast road between Tākaka and Collingwood, looking out over Parapara Inlet and the long sweep of Golden Bay toward Farewell Spit. It is twenty minutes from Tākaka and ten from Collingwood, with a beach, an estuary full of wading birds and very little else. If your idea of a holiday involves a book, a deck and no neighbours, this is the stretch of coast to look at.
body:
Both of our Parapara homes look out over the water — one from the beachfront, one from up in the bush on the hill — and that view is generally why people book. It suits couples and small families who want to swim, walk and read, then drive to whatever takes their fancy: Wharariki Beach and the Farewell Spit tours are about forty-five minutes north, Te Waikoropupū Springs and the Tākaka cafés twenty minutes south.

The inlet is the local secret. On a rising tide it fills fast and turns into a warm, shallow swimming hole; on a falling one it becomes a bird table — oystercatchers, herons and, from spring through summer, godwits feeding on the flats. Bring binoculars, and bring repellent: the estuary edge earns its sandflies at dawn and dusk in still weather.
highlights: Halfway along the coast road: Tākaka 20 minutes one way, Collingwood 10 the other
Parapara Inlet — warm, shallow water on a rising tide and wading birds on a falling one
Open views across Golden Bay to Farewell Spit
No streetlights, so the Milky Way shows on any clear night
About 45 minutes to Wharariki Beach and the Farewell Spit tour departures

faqs.q: Is there a shop at Parapara?
faqs.a: No. Collingwood, ten minutes north, has a general store, fuel and a couple of places to eat; Tākaka, twenty minutes south, has the supermarket and pharmacy. Most guests do one shop on the way in and top up in Collingwood.

faqs.q: Can you swim at Parapara?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is best around high tide. The beach and the inlet both drain to sandflats on a big low, so aim for the two or three hours either side of high water when the incoming tide has warmed over the sand.

faqs.q: What birds will we see on the inlet?
faqs.a: Variable oystercatchers, white-faced herons, pied stilts and shags are there most of the year, and bar-tailed godwits feed on the flats through the warmer months before flying north. Golden Bay and Farewell Spit sit on one of the great shorebird migrations, and Parapara is a quiet front-row seat for it.

faqs.q: How dark does it get at night?
faqs.a: Properly dark. There is no street lighting on this part of the coast road and very little traffic after dinner, so on a clear night you can pick out the Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds from the deck.

name: Onekaka
headline: Holiday homes at Onekakā
metaDescription: Onekaka holiday accommodation on the Golden Bay coast road — rural quiet, the Mussel Inn up the road, 15 minutes from both Takaka and Collingwood.
intro: Onekakā is a rural stretch of coast about fifteen minutes north of Tākaka, known for two things. The first is the Mussel Inn, Golden Bay's much-loved bush pub and brewery, which sits on SH60 here. The second is the ironworks that operated in the 1920s and 30s — the remains of its long wharf still stand out in the tide, one of the odder pieces of industrial history on this coast.
body:
We look after one home here, a four-bedroom villa above the Ōtere with views out over the bay, and it works best for groups who want a rural base within reach of both ends of Golden Bay: Tākaka is fifteen minutes south, Collingwood fifteen minutes north, and the beaches at Patons Rock and Parapara are five and ten minutes up the road. What guests write afterwards is almost always about having the place to themselves.

Onekakā is farmland, river and bush rather than a beach strip, so days tend to look like a morning at Patons Rock, an afternoon on the Pupū Hydro Walkway or at Te Waikoropupū Springs, and dinner and live music at the Mussel Inn. There are no shops here at all — do the supermarket run in Tākaka on the way in, and check opening hours before you plan a meal out in the off-season.
highlights: The Mussel Inn — bush pub, in-house brewery and regular live music — is on the main road here
Remains of the 1920s Onekakā ironworks wharf sit out in the tide
Fifteen minutes to Tākaka and fifteen to Collingwood: central for day trips both ways
Patons Rock beach is about five minutes north, Parapara about ten
Rural and quiet — river, farmland and bush rather than a beach settlement

faqs.q: How far is Onekakā from Takaka?
faqs.a: About 13 km, or fifteen minutes on SH60. Tākaka has the supermarket, fuel, pharmacy and most of the Bay's cafés, and it is also where you turn off for Te Waikoropupū Springs on the way through.

faqs.q: What is the Mussel Inn?
faqs.a: A Golden Bay institution on the main road at Onekakā: a rough-sawn timber bar that has brewed its own beer and cider since the early 1990s, with an open fire, a big garden and live music through the summer. Its mānuka-flavoured Captain Cooker is the one visitors are told to try. Hours shrink outside summer, so check before you drive out.

faqs.q: Is there a beach at Onekakā?
faqs.a: There is coastline rather than a swimming beach — this stretch is tidal flats, with the old ironworks wharf piles visible at low water. For sand, Patons Rock is about five minutes north and Pōhara is around twenty-five minutes east.

faqs.q: Can we stay at Onekakā without a car?
faqs.a: Not realistically. There is no public transport in Golden Bay and no shops within walking distance, so you will need a vehicle here — as you will almost everywhere in the Bay outside Tākaka township.

name: East Takaka
headline: Holiday homes in East Tākaka
metaDescription: East Takaka holiday accommodation in Golden Bay's inland valley — farmhouse space for big groups, 10 minutes to Takaka, at the bottom of the Rameka Track.
intro: East Tākaka is the farming valley that runs inland from Tākaka township toward the foot of Takaka Hill — ten minutes from the supermarket and a world away from the beach settlements. This is marble country: bush-covered hills, the Tākaka River, fog lifting off the paddocks in the morning, and birdsong instead of traffic. It is also the first place you reach once you have come down off the hill.
body:
The home we look after here is a farmhouse that sleeps ten, which makes East Tākaka the obvious pick for reunions, milestone birthdays and groups who would rather have one kitchen and one long table than three baches spread across a beach. Guests write about the space and the silence — kids running loose in the paddocks, cooking at home every night, not seeing another car all day.

It is also the mountain-biking end of the valley. The Rameka Track drops off Takaka Hill into East Tākaka and is one of the oldest and best-loved descents in the country, and the Rawhiti Cave track starts at the end of Packard Road just up the valley. Paynes Ford — Golden Bay's main climbing crag, with swimming holes in the river below it — is about five minutes away on the road back into town.
highlights: Ten minutes to Tākaka township, and the first valley you reach coming down Takaka Hill
Bottom of the Rameka Track, the classic Takaka Hill mountain-bike descent
Rawhiti Cave, with its phototropic stalactites growing toward the light, is up Packard Road
Paynes Ford climbing crag and river swimming holes are about five minutes away
Farm-and-bush setting: no through traffic, big skies, tūī and bellbirds at dawn

faqs.q: How far is East Tākaka from the beach?
faqs.a: Pōhara is about twenty minutes and Tata Beach about twenty-five. You are inland here, and the trade-off is space, quiet and paddocks instead of a shared beach access.

faqs.q: Is East Tākaka suitable for a large group?
faqs.a: It is one of the best options in Golden Bay for one. The farmhouse sleeps ten, and because the nearest neighbours are paddocks away it is a far easier fit for a noisy family week than a bach in the middle of a beach settlement.

faqs.q: What is there to do nearby?
faqs.a: The Rawhiti Cave track is a steep 45-minute climb from the end of Packard Road to one of the most spectacular cave entrances in New Zealand. Paynes Ford has climbing and river swimming, the Rameka is on the doorstep for riders, and Te Waikoropupū Springs is about twenty minutes away through town.

faqs.q: Do we need a four-wheel drive?
faqs.a: No. East Tākaka Road is sealed, and a normal car is fine for getting to the house. A few of the side roads to trailheads are gravel and can be rutted after heavy rain, so take those slowly.
